source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP look-back techniques to solve real-world SAT instances
finding: Adds conflict-directed backjumping (CBJ) and learning of derived reasons (nogoods) to a Davis-Putnam solver (relsat). Learning is limited: size-bounded keeps nogoods with i or fewer variables; relevance-bounded keeps a nogood only while at most i of its variables changed since it was derived. Tested on planning, scheduling and circuit instances.
numbers: Unenhanced DP (naivesat) failed 100% of runs at a 10 minute cutoff on both bf1355-075 and ssa2670-141. CBJ alone solved bf1355-075 in all 100 runs. 100 random-seed runs per instance, SPARC-10.
quote: Relevance-bounded learning of order i maintains any reason that contains at most i variables whose assignments have changed since the reason was derived.
limits: Instances were picked for difficulty. Run-time variance was extremely high between seeds, so means hide a lot. Some table cells are unreadable in the PDF text.
agent_relevance: A failed attempt can be cut down to a short reason and kept only while it still applies. Relevance-based forgetting is a ready rule for our no-good store.

source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP look-back techniques to solve real-world SAT instances - hard circuit instance ssa2670-141
finding: On the single-stuck-at circuit instance, plain CBJ still failed in some runs; learning fixed that. Relevance-bounded learning gave a clear speedup. Fourth-order size-bounded learning pruned more but was slower from overhead.
numbers: Failures at 10 min cutoff over 100 runs: naivesat 100%, cbjsat 23, sizesat(3) 23% (415 s), sizesat(4) 0% (242 s), relsat(3) 4% (278 s), relsat(4) 0%. POSIT reported 50 s by Freeman; ntab_back 1,353 s.
limits: Instance is unsatisfiable. Cross-machine time comparisons are rough (SPARC-10 vs other machines).
agent_relevance: More memory of past failures (up to a limit) cut failure rate from 100% to 0% on a hard instance. There is a cost curve: longer no-goods cost more to keep.

source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP look-back techniques to solve real-world SAT instances - planning instance hanoi4/hanoi5
finding: Tower-of-Hanoi planning encodings have deep local minima. Only the strongest learning variant solved them reliably. relsat(4) solved the open hanoi5 instance, which no SAT algorithm was known to have solved.
numbers: hanoi4 failure rate at cutoff: sizesat(3) 94%, sizesat(4) 92%, relsat(3) 79%, relsat(4) 13%. hanoi5: only relsat(4) solved it, in 4 of 100 runs, under 3 minutes mean on those runs. ntab_back needed 2,877 s on hanoi4 and failed hanoi5 in 12 hours.
limits: Low success rate on hanoi5; a cutoff of 10 minutes was used. Authors say longer cutoffs would likely help.
agent_relevance: Learned no-goods make hard planning-like search tractable where plain backtracking stalls. Relevance-bounded memory beats size-bounded memory on planning.

source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP look-back techniques to solve real-world SAT instances - boundary conditions
finding: Learning is not a universal win. Short, easily derived nogoods are what help. Random 3SAT phase-transition instances have short nogoods that need deep inference, and look-back gave little. Local search and simple randomized sampling beat it on some families.
numbers: 3bit circuit instances: never solved by any DP variant, trivial for WSAT. 2bitadd_10 (unsat): needed 18 hours with relsat(4). ISAMP solved 6 scheduling instances an order of magnitude faster than relsat(4) with 100% success. relsat(4) failed 17-21% on two scheduling instances and on 4blocks at 10 min.
quote: Real-world instances often contain subproblems with short, easily derived nogoods.
limits: Authors' explanation (synergy of look-ahead heuristics with learned clauses) is a conjecture, not tested.
agent_relevance: No-goods help when failures share small reasons. Where failure reasons are long or diffuse, a no-good store adds cost and little benefit.

source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP look-back techniques to solve real-world SAT instances - versus WSAT and Tableau (Table 4)
finding: Against stochastic local search (WSAT) and Tableau with backjumping on Kautz-Selman planning encodings, relsat(4) was far faster than Tableau and often faster than WSAT, but WSAT won on some direct encodings.
numbers: Seconds, relsat(4) / WSAT / ntab_back: log_gp.c 39.4 / 419.2 / 11,144; bw_dir.d 813.3 / 1,499 / over 12 hours; log_dir.b 16.6 / 2.6 / 161.4. 100 runs, 10 min cutoff.
limits: WSAT times from a 110 MHz SGI, normalised by the authors; relsat is complete, WSAT cannot prove unsat.
agent_relevance: Learning-based systematic search can match local search on planning, so a scaffold that records failures need not give up completeness.

source: Marques-Silva and Sakallah (1996) GRASP: a new search algorithm for satisfiability (ICCAD)
finding: Founding CDCL paper. Treats conflicts as inevitable and analyzes each one. A backward walk over the implication graph (nodes are assignments, edges come from the clause that forced each implication) finds the assignments that caused the conflict. Three outputs: a new conflict-induced clause (added to avoid the same conflict), a failure-driven assertion if the cause is the latest decision, or a non-chronological jump back if the cause is an earlier decision.
numbers: Backtrack level formula: go back to the highest decision level among the cause assignments. Soundness and completeness proofs cited to technical reports.
quote: considers the occurrence of a conflict ... as an opportunity to learn from the mistake that led to the conflict
limits: Paper is 8 pages and defers proofs and full evaluation to a technical report. Conflict analysis adds noticeable overhead.
agent_relevance: This is the exact template for a no-good: name the few assignments that caused the failure, store their negation, jump back to the earliest relevant choice.

source: Marques-Silva and Sakallah (1996) GRASP: a new search algorithm for satisfiability (ICCAD) - bounding growth and unique implication points
finding: Clause-database growth can be exponential. Fix: clauses of size at most k are kept (green); longer ones (red) are kept only while unit, giving polynomial worst-case growth. Dominator nodes of the conflict vertex (unique implication points, UIPs) give stronger, shorter clauses and can be found in linear time.
numbers: In experiments clauses were limited to 20 literals or fewer. Adding larger clauses helped until overhead offset gains.
limits: Details of the growth study are in a tech report that was not opened.
agent_relevance: Cap no-good length and prefer the shortest explanation that still forces a different choice.

source: Marques-Silva and Sakallah (1996) GRASP: a new search algorithm for satisfiability (ICCAD) - experimental results (Table 1)
finding: On UCSC circuit-fault and DIMACS benchmarks GRASP finished far more instances than TEGUS and POSIT. 10,000 CPU second limit per instance.
numbers: BF-1355: GRASP 149 of 149 in 125.7 s total; TEGUS 53 solved; POSIT 64 solved (946,127 s). SSA-2670: GRASP 12 of 12 in 51.5 s; TEGUS 0 of 12. BF-2670: GRASP 53 of 53 in 68.3 s; TEGUS 25 solved.
limits: Sparse CNF from circuits suits BCP-based conflict analysis. Author-run comparison against older tools.
agent_relevance: Gains are largest on structured, sparse problems where failures have local causes.

source: Marques-Silva and Sakallah (1996) GRASP: a new search algorithm for satisfiability (ICCAD) - where it did not win
finding: POSIT or TEGUS were faster on some classes, mostly small or satisfiable ones. GRASP overhead shows on easy instances. Some classes were unsolved by every tool.
numbers: AIM-50: GRASP 0.4 s, POSIT 0.4 s; II-8: GRASP 23.4 s vs POSIT 2.3 s; JNH: GRASP 21.3 s vs POSIT 0.8 s; PAR-32 and classes F, G unsolved by all three at the limit; II-16: GRASP 9 of 10.
limits: TEGUS iterates several decision procedures, which helps on satisfiable instances.
agent_relevance: Conflict learning has fixed overhead. For easy tasks a no-good store is wasted effort.

source: Marques-Silva and Sakallah (1996) GRASP: a new search algorithm for satisfiability (ICCAD) - conflict statistics (Table 2)
finding: Non-chronological backtracks were a significant share of all backtracks, and some jumps potentially skip millions of tree nodes. Clause database growth was not necessarily large. UIPs occurred in practice.
numbers: Table columns: #B backtracks, #NCB non-chronological, #LJ largest jump, #UIP, %G database growth. Exact values not extracted here.
limits: Statistics given for selected DIMACS instances only.
agent_relevance: Backjumping, not only clause storage, carries the saving; skipping irrelevant choices is a main source of pruning.

source: Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang, Malik (2001) Chaff: engineering an efficient SAT solver
finding: Chaff made CDCL fast with engineering, not new learning theory. Most of a solver's run time is in unit propagation, so Chaff used two watched literals per clause so backtracking needs no clause updates.
numbers: More than 90 percent of run time in most cases is spent in BCP.
limits: PDF read from a two-column text extraction; some lines are cut.
agent_relevance: Cheap bookkeeping for the no-good store matters as much as what is stored.

source: Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang, Malik (2001) Chaff: engineering an efficient SAT solver - VSIDS and restarts
finding: VSIDS: a counter per literal, raised when it appears in a new conflict clause, periodically shrunk by a constant, so decisions focus on recent conflicts. Restarts clear all decisions but keep learned clauses, so the solver does not repeat the same analysis. Thousands of restarts are possible on a hard instance, though similar results can sometimes come without restarts. Restart period grows over time to keep completeness.
numbers: Chaff finished large instances in one to two orders of magnitude less time than the best public solvers. On SSS.1.0 about an order of magnitude faster. Tested on almost a thousand formulas, Sun UltraSparc II.
quote: a restart consists of clearing the state of all the variables ... any still-relevant clauses ... are still present after the restart
limits: Authors attribute the speedup to optimized BCP plus a decision strategy focused on recent clauses, not to sophisticated learning. No ablation of restarts alone was reported.
agent_relevance: Restart while keeping the no-goods is the pattern: change the early choices, keep the lessons.

source: Katebi, Sakallah, Marques-Silva (2011) Empirical study of the anatomy of modern SAT solvers
finding: Ablation of MiniSat: turn off one of four features at a time and count instances solved within 1000 s. Order of importance: clause learning, then VSIDS, then two watched literals, then restarts.
numbers: 10,000 runs per configuration (about 150,000 runs in all, ten shuffled copies per benchmark). Solved: full CDCL 9,068; no learning 4,837; no VSIDS (DLIS) 6,932; no two-watched-literals 8,409; no restarts 8,653.
limits: Single solver (MiniSat) and one benchmark mix. Authors note a feature's presence does not always beat its absence.
agent_relevance: Evidence that stored lessons are the biggest single contributor, larger than the search heuristic and far larger than restarts.

source: Katebi, Sakallah, Marques-Silva (2011) Empirical study of the anatomy of modern SAT solvers - families where the ranking breaks
finding: Per-family results show learning is not always best. On some families turning a feature off solved more.
numbers: Crypto family (300 runs): no learning 472 vs full CDCL 237 (column order as extracted from a garbled table; likely but confirm). sverif (500): no VSIDS 592 vs full CDCL 420. plan (1200): no learning 327, full 1006. atpg: 965 without learning vs 1000 with.
limits: Crypto column reading depends on garbled PDF text; treat the crypto result as likely but check.
agent_relevance: Domain matters: on unstructured or hash-like problems, stored no-goods may not pay.

source: Audemard and Simon (2009) Predicting learnt clauses quality in modern SAT solvers (Glucose)
finding: Observation: on industrial instances the decision level at which conflicts occur decreases over the run, i.e., learning makes the solver reach contradictions higher in the tree. A least-squares line through (conflict number, decision level) predicts when the solver finishes.
numbers: Regression slope was negative on 167 of 199 benchmarks. The predicted finish ('look-back justification') was between 0.90 and 8.33 times the real conflict count, mostly about 1.37 times. Not seen on random problems; the crypto 'mizh' series was 100 percent increasing.
limits: Linear fit is admitted to be false in most cases; it shows correlation, not cause.
agent_relevance: A usable progress signal: if lessons are working, failures should come earlier (higher in the tree). We could track failure depth as a stall detector.

source: Audemard and Simon (2009) Predicting learnt clauses quality in modern SAT solvers (Glucose) - literal block distance and aggressive deletion
finding: LBD of a learned clause is the number of distinct decision levels among its literals. Clauses with LBD 2 ('glue clauses') are used far more than long ones. LBD of the first-UIP clause is the smallest among all UIP choices. Aggressive deletion: every 20,000 + 500x conflicts (x = times done) remove half the learned clauses, keeping asserting ones and low LBD.
numbers: Table 2: average uses of a clause by LBD group, about 202 propagation and 1,827 conflict-analysis uses for the lowest-LBD column versus 26 and 136 for LBD 4 (column mapping from text). Glucose solved 176 of 234 SAT'07 industrial instances in 10,000 s; PicoSat 153; RSat 139; MiniSat 132; about 140 for others. Fastest on 68 cases, at least 1.2 times faster on common instances; 140 solved in 2,500 s.
quote: LBD of FUIP learnt clause is optimal over all other UIPs
limits: Compared with 2007-era solvers on preprocessed instances; gain is mostly on UNSAT.
agent_relevance: A cheap quality score for a stored lesson: how many separate decision groups does it tie together. Keep tight, cross-level lessons; drop the rest.

source: Liang, Ganesh, Zulkoski, Zaman, Czarnecki (2015) Understanding VSIDS branching heuristics in CDCL SAT solvers
finding: Explains why VSIDS works. It overwhelmingly bumps and picks 'bridge' variables that link communities of the instance. Multiplicative decay acts like an exponential moving average, favoring recent conflicts. VSIDS ranking correlates with temporal graph centrality of learned clauses.
numbers: Tests on 1,030 SAT Competition 2013 instances, 5,000 s timeout, modified MiniSat. A new adaptive-decay variant (adaptVSIDS) solved 351 instances versus 343 for mVSIDS, 2.4 percent more.
limits: Correlational; community structure in random instances is absent so findings hold for application and crafted families only.
agent_relevance: Recency-weighted attention to what failed lately is a principled way to pick what to try next.

source: Beame, Kautz, Sabharwal (2004) Towards understanding and harnessing the potential of clause learning (JAIR 22)
finding: First precise proof-system model of clause learning (CL). Shows CL can give exponentially shorter proofs than regular resolution and Davis-Putnam resolution, using a new FirstNewCut scheme on trace-extended formulas. A CL variant with unlimited restarts is as strong as general resolution. Any CL proof, whatever the scheme or restarts, can be simulated by resolution.
numbers: Theorem 1: exponential separation from every proper 'natural' refinement of resolution. Proof uses a proof trace extension that adds a variable per clause.
quote: with a new learning scheme, CL can provide exponentially shorter proofs than many proper refinements of general resolution
limits: Results hold for a nondeterministic solver that picks the best branching and restarts; real solvers have no such oracle. FirstNewCut is a theoretical scheme.
agent_relevance: Learning plus a good choice order is what gives power. Order of attempts matters as much as storing failures.

source: Beame, Kautz, Sabharwal (2004) Towards understanding and harnessing the potential of clause learning (JAIR 22) - guided branching experiments
finding: Branching order given from a high-level problem description (the pebbling graph) turned hard formulas easy for zChaff. Clause learning alone, with the default heuristic, failed on small ones.
numbers: 1.6 GHz Athlon, 6 hour limit, zChaff 2001.6.15 with restarts off. Unmodified zChaff passed 6 hours at about 7 to 8 layers (under 100 variables). With the generated sequence, grid pebbling solved at 1,000 layers (1,001,000 variables): 4,251 s unsat, 5,335 s sat. Randomized pebbling: 13,324 nodes (1.7 million clauses) in 669 s unsat.
limits: Needs the structure of the problem as input. Table layout in the PDF text is partly garbled. Authors call these a proof of concept.
agent_relevance: Where problem structure is known, handing the solver a good order of attempts beats leaving it to learned heuristics alone.

source: Buss, Hoffmann, Johannsen (2008) Resolution trees with lemmas (LMCS 4)
finding: Exact proof-system match for DPLL with learning. DPLL with learning by unit propagation is simulated by regular resolution trees with input lemmas (regWRTI); the general form 'DLL-Learn' equals regular WRTL. Variable extensions let these simulate general resolution without restarts.
numbers: Regular dag resolution is exponentially separated from regWRTI. Lower bound: exponential for WRTL when lemmas are restricted to short clauses.
limits: Pure theory; no runtimes. Learning order and extra variables are idealized.
agent_relevance: Short-lemma limits are formal: if we cap lesson length too hard, some tasks become provably exponential.

source: Atserias, Fichte, Thurley (2011) Clause-learning algorithms with many restarts and bounded-width resolution (JAIR 40)
finding: For a concrete randomized solver (unit propagation to saturation before each decision, learning, restarts), with high probability it behaves like width-k resolution after at most O(n^(2k+2)) conflicts and restarts, where n is the number of variables. So restarts plus learning plus a little randomness already do bounded-width reasoning.
numbers: Upper bound O(k^2 ln(kn) n^(2k+1)) conflicts for the main variant. Needs restarts often enough and random decisions.
limits: Polynomial bound has a huge exponent; it is an existence result, not a speed prediction.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal reason to restart and keep lessons: repeated cheap tries with memory reach all short-reason refutations.

source: Pipatsrisawat and Darwiche (2008) A new clause learning scheme for efficient unsatisfiability proofs (AAAI)
finding: Formal model of a modern CDCL solver and a property called empowerment: a learned clause is useful if adding it lets unit propagation derive something it could not before. All asserting clauses are empowering. Bi-asserting clauses (two literals at the conflict level) are shorter and jump further, but only help if empowering.
numbers: 949 problems, 1,800 s each. UNSAT solved: Rsat 402, Rsat+ 433, Rsat++ 438 (+36). UNSAT time on commonly solved: 71,246 s to 47,400 s (-34 percent). Bi-asserting clause about half the size of asserting; backtrack 5 to 6 times longer. Not checking empowerment: only 647 solved versus 740 for plain Rsat.
quote: adding a conflict clause that is not 1-empowering to the knowledge base will not lead to any new implication
limits: SAT instances: Rsat+ was slightly worse. Empowerment is checked only against clauses used in the derivation (about 95 percent of problems had over 80 percent truly empowering).
agent_relevance: Direct test of which no-goods deserve to be kept: only those that unlock a new inference. Keeping short but useless lessons made the solver worse (647 vs 740).

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting combinatorial search through randomization (AAAI)
finding: Run time of a complete search on one instance is heavy-tailed: there is a real chance a run needs exponentially longer than any seen before. Hardness lives in the pairing of instance and deterministic heuristic, not the instance alone. Random restarts with a cutoff remove the right tail and exploit lucky short runs on the left.
numbers: Table 1 (deterministic vs randomized mean): logistics.d Satz 108 min vs 95 s at cutoff 16 backtracks (about 1,800 backtracks total); 3bit-adder-32 over 24 h vs 95 s; round-robin 16 over 24 h vs 250 s; round-robin 18 over 48 h vs 1.4 h. A tail index of 1.5 gives a finite mean but infinite variance.
quote: hardness did not reside in the instances, but in the combination of the instance with the details of the deterministic algorithm
limits: Not universal: round-robin 14 got worse (411 s vs 17 min) and blocks-world showed no heavy tail (30 min vs about 23 min). Cutoff must be tuned.
agent_relevance: Restarts matter because of luck in early choices; this is the justification for restart-with-memory, and it warns that blind restarts help only when the tail is heavy.

source: Elffers, Giraldez-Cru, Gocht, Nordstrom, Simon (2018) Seeking practical CDCL insights from theoretical SAT benchmarks (IJCAI)
finding: Used scalable, theoretically easy formulas (short resolution proofs) with solver knobs to see how heuristics affect proof search. Learned clauses are critical for the jump from tree-like to general resolution proofs. Frequent restarts help on some families. Adaptive (Glucose-style) restarts often beat Luby restarts but sometimes are switched off by accident, causing terrible performance. LBD helps when memory is tight. VSIDS decay factor can matter a lot. No support found that the learning-rate branching heuristic beats VSIDS.
numbers: Findings are qualitative, from PAR-score comparisons over knob combinations. Cites Katebi et al. that learning and conflict-directed branching account for most of the gain over DPLL.
limits: Crafted benchmarks, not industrial; authors stress correlation is not causation. URL is the proceedings index, not the exact paper link.
agent_relevance: Confirms that stored lessons, not search tricks, give the qualitative leap, while restart and forgetting policy needs care.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning (bridge to LLM side)
finding: Only the abstract-level claims and a few grepped lines were seen, not the full text. Agent stores a written reflection after failure and reads it on the next attempt, loosely like a learned clause. Covered fully by the LLM-agent angle.
numbers: Reported: ALFWorld ReAct + Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks; HumanEval pass@1 91 percent versus 80 percent for GPT-4 baseline; +22 percent ALFWorld, +20 percent HotPotQA, +11 percent HumanEval (absolute, authors' claims).
limits: Not read in depth by this angle. Reflections are free text, with no check that they are implied by the failure, unlike CDCL clauses which are logically implied by the formula.
agent_relevance: Key gap versus CDCL: a SAT no-good is provably sound and checkable; an LLM reflection is not. A scaffold should store lessons only in checkable form where possible.
